Addressing modes determine how operands are accessed during instruction execution, and examples are immediate addressing, direct addressing, indirect addressing and register addressing

Real-life applications of addressing modes are efficient program execution, where compilers choose addressing modes to optimize speed, embedded systems, where efficient memory access is crucial in devices with limited memory, and gaming systems, where fast memory access improves frame rates and responsiveness
Registers are small, fast storage locations inside the CPU, and their types include general-purpose registers and special-purpose registers such as the Program Counter and the Stack Pointer

Programs execute faster when data is stored in registers instead of memory, critical real-time systems such as air traffic control rely on fast register operations, and efficient register usage improves battery life and performance in mobile devices
Computer organization deals with how architectural features are physically implemented, and the first of its components is the control unit
The control unit coordinates all operations of the CPU by fetching instructions, decoding instructions and generating control signals

Real-life applications of the control unit are processor execution, where every program relies on the control unit, industrial automation, where machines operate based on control signals, and robotics systems, where it controls sensors and actuators
The Arithmetic Logic Unit performs arithmetic operations such as addition and subtraction and logical operations such as AND, OR and NOT

Real-life applications of the ALU are digital calculators, gaming systems whose physics calculations depend on it, and artificial intelligence systems whose neural network computations involve massive arithmetic operations
Memory is organized hierarchically as cache, which is fastest, then main memory or RAM, then secondary storage

Real-life applications of memory organization are smartphones, whose faster app performance depends on an efficient memory hierarchy, web browsers, where cache memory speeds up page loading, and cloud systems, where efficient memory usage supports large-scale computing
Input/output systems handle communication between the computer and external devices

Real-life applications of I/O systems are user interaction through keyboard input and monitor output, medical devices where sensors provide input and displays provide output, and smart homes where devices communicate with environmental sensors
Buses transfer data, addresses and control signals, and the three types are the data bus, the address bus and the control bus

Real-life applications of system buses are motherboard communication, where all components communicate via buses, gaming computers, where high-speed buses improve graphics performance, and servers, where efficient data transfer supports multiple users
Pipelining is the overlapping of instruction execution while parallelism is the executing of multiple tasks simultaneously

Real-life applications of pipelining and parallelism are modern CPUs, which execute multiple instructions at once, multicore processors, which enable multitasking, and AI and big data systems, which handle massive computations efficiently
Sequential access reads locations one after the other in sequence, and its example is magnetic tape
Random access means all locations can be accessed in constant time, and its example is RAM
Direct access works like locating a street, finding the vicinity or block first, and its example is the hard disk drive
Associative access holds the address and the content together, and its example is cache
Computer memory exhibits a number of characteristics: location, access methods, performance such as transfer rate, and capacity or size
Memory hierarchy is a structured arrangement of different storage types in a computer system, designed to optimize performance and cost
The memory trade-off is that faster access time means greater cost per bit, greater capacity means slower access, and smaller cost per bit means slower access
Design constraints on memory can be summed up by three questions: how much space, how fast is the access time, and how expensive
On capacity, if memory exists then applications will likely be developed to use it
Best performance is achieved when memory keeps up with the processor, so that as the processor executes instructions the memory minimizes pausing or waiting for instructions or operands
The cost of memory must be reasonable in relationship to other components
The way out of the memory dilemma is not to rely on a single memory but to employ a memory hierarchy, supplementing smaller, more expensive, faster memories with larger, cheaper, slower memories
As one goes down the memory hierarchy the cost per bit decreases, capacity increases and access time increases
As one goes down the memory hierarchy the frequency of access of memory by the processor decreases, which is very key to the performance of the CPU
The typical memory hierarchy from top to bottom is Level 1 Registers, Level 2 Cache Memory, Level 3 Main Memory (RAM), Level 4 Secondary Storage (SSD or HDD) and Level 5 Tertiary Storage
In the hierarchy table registers are fastest, highest in cost and smallest in capacity, while tertiary storage is slowest, lowest in cost and very large in capacity
In the hierarchy table cache memory is very fast, high in cost and small, while main memory is moderate in speed, medium in cost and medium in capacity
The lecture poses the in-class question: why do we not use only cache memory in a computer system?
We do not use only cache memory because cache is very expensive and has limited capacity
Spatial locality means that if we access a memory location, close by addresses will very likely be accessed, as in a loop operation
Temporal locality means that if we access a memory location, we will very likely access it again
Locality of reference is a consequence of using iterative loops and subroutines, because instructions and data will be accessed multiple times
In the two-level worked example, Level 1 contains 1000 words or bytes with an access time of 0.01 microseconds and Level 2 contains 100,000 words or bytes with an access time of 0.1 microseconds
In the two-level example, if the word is in L1 the processor accesses it directly in 0.01 microseconds, and if it is in L2 the word is first transferred to L1 and then accessed, costing 0.01 plus 0.1

In the two-level example H is the fraction of all memory accesses that are found in L1, T1 is the access time to L1 and T2 is the access time to L2, and the time for the processor to determine which level holds the word is ignored for simplicity
For high percentages of L1 access, the average total access time is much closer to that of L1 than that of L2
If 95% of memory accesses are found in L1, the average time to access a word is 0.95 times 0.01 plus 0.05 times 0.01 plus 0.1, which is 0.0095 plus 0.0055, giving 0.015 microseconds
The strategy to minimize accesses is to organize data across the hierarchy so that the percentage of accesses to lower levels is substantially less than that to upper levels

L2 holds all program instructions and data, data currently being used is held in L1, and eventually data in L1 is swapped out to L2 to make room for new data, so that on average most references are to data in L1
Processor registers are the fastest, smallest and most expensive type of memory
The cache stages data movement between registers and main memory, improves performance, and is not usually visible to the processor or to the programmer
Main memory is the principal internal memory system of the computer, and each of its locations has a unique address

Cache memory is designed to combine the memory access time of expensive, high-speed memory with the large memory size of less expensive, lower-speed memory, and it contains a copy of portions of main memory
Cache can be 1 to 2 MB while main memory can be up to 64 GB
A nibble is 4 bits and a byte is 8 bits
A word is one or more complete rows of memory and a block is a collection of words, typically 2, 4 or 8
A memory size of 4 MB works out as 4 times 1024 times 1024 times 8, which is 33,554,432 bits, and 10 KB works out as 10 times 1024 times 8, which is 81,920 bits
When the processor attempts to read a word of memory a check is made to determine if the word is in the cache, and if it is, a cache hit, the word is delivered to the processor
On a cache miss the block of main memory that contains the word is read into the cache, and the cache then delivers the word to the processor
Because of the locality of reference principle, when a block of data is fetched into the cache it is likely that there will be future references to that same memory location
The cache concept is improved by introducing multiple levels of cache: L2 cache is slower and typically larger than L1 cache, and L3 cache is slower and typically larger than L2 cache
Main memory consists of 2 to the power n addressable words, each word having a unique n-bit address, and the memory consists of a number of fixed-length blocks of K words each
The number of main memory blocks is M equals 2 to the power n divided by K
Cache memory consists of m blocks called lines, each line contains K words, and each line also includes control bits
If a word in a block of memory is read, the whole block is transferred to a cache line
Because m is much less than M, the cache cannot permanently store a block, so it needs to identify the block stored, and that information is held in the tag field
In the cache read operation the processor generates the read address RA of the word to be read, and if the word is in the cache it is delivered to the processor
Otherwise the block containing that word is loaded into the cache and the word is delivered to the processor, these last two operations occurring in parallel

The cache connects to the processor via data, control and address lines, and the data and address lines also attach to data and address buffers, which attach to a system bus from which main memory is reached
When a cache hit occurs the data and address buffers are disabled, communication is only between processor and cache, and there is no system bus traffic
When a cache miss occurs the desired address is loaded onto the system bus and the data are returned through the data buffer to both the cache and the processor
There are two types of cache addresses: physical addresses, which are actual memory addresses, and logical addresses, which are virtual-memory addresses
Virtual memory performs mapping between the logical addresses used by a program and physical addresses, and its main idea is to disregard the amount of main memory available
A virtual cache stores data using logical addresses, so the processor accesses the cache directly without going through the MMU
The advantage of a virtual cache is faster access speed, since the cache can respond without the need for an MMU address translation

The disadvantage of a virtual cache is that the same virtual address in two different applications refers to two different physical addresses, so the cache must be flushed at each application context switch, or extra bits must be added to each cache line to identify which virtual address space the address refers to

Cache size should be small enough that the overall average cost per bit is close to that of main memory alone, and large enough that the overall average access time is close to that of the cache alone
The larger the cache the more complex the addressing logic, with the result that large caches tend to be slightly slower than small ones, and available chip and board area also limits cache size
A processor is the logic circuitry that responds to and processes the basic instructions that drive a computer
CPU instructions are numbers stored in memory
An instruction set is the set of instructions a programmer can give to a machine to perform operations, and the instructions are specific to the CPU architecture
The basic operations of a processor are: read instruction from memory, decode, execute, write back
Two major processor design philosophies emerged over the years: Complex Instruction Set Computer (CISC) and Reduced Instruction Set Computer (RISC)
During the 1960s and 1970s memory was expensive while processor hardware was relatively cheap
Engineers attempted to reduce program size by creating processors with powerful instructions capable of performing complex tasks in a single instruction, which led to CISC architectures
By the early 1980s researchers discovered that most programs used only a small subset of the available instructions
Researchers found that complex instructions often required multiple clock cycles while simpler instructions could be executed much faster, and this observation led to RISC architectures
The lecture poses the in-class question: why were CISC architectures initially popular?
CISC architectures were initially popular because memory was expensive, and CISC instructions could perform complex operations using fewer instructions, thereby reducing program size
CISC existed close to the beginning of general computing, when the earliest machines were programmed in assembly language and memory was slow and expensive
IBM designed an instruction set to allow early programmers to easily program a hundred complex instructions rather than thousands of individual instructions
CISC was developed to make compiler development simpler: it shifts most of the burden of generating machine instructions to the processor
Instead of a compiler writing long machine instructions to calculate a square root, a CISC processor would have a built-in ability to do this

Complex instruction set computing is a CPU design where single instructions can execute several low-level operations, such as a load from memory, an arithmetic operation and a memory store, or are capable of multi-step operations or addressing modes within single instructions
CISC is called complex because of the complex work performed per instruction, and its concept is to encode the intention directly, as in add X and Y and put the result in Z
The problem with CISC is that some instructions take more time than others
Examples of CISC architectures are x86 and s390, and CISC has a small number of general purpose registers
Computers typically use CISC while tablets, smartphones and other devices use RISC
The higher efficiency of the RISC architecture makes it desirable in applications where cycles and power are usually in short supply
In CISC, instructions are executed by microcode
A CISC instruction set typically includes many instructions with different sizes and execution cycles, which makes CISC instructions harder to pipeline
A CISC processor has a large number of instructions, typically from 100 to 250 instructions
A CISC processor has a large variety of addressing modes, typically 5 to 20 different modes
A CISC processor includes some instructions that perform specialized tasks and are used infrequently
CISC characteristics include variable-length instruction formats and instructions that manipulate operands in memory
Properties of a CISC processor: a richer instruction set, some simple and some very complex, and instructions of a variable size
CISC instructions generally take more than 1 clock to execute
A CISC processor interfaces with memory in multiple mechanisms with complex addressing modes, and has no pipelining
Microcode control makes the CISC instruction set possible and flexible, and CISC works well with a simpler compiler
An advantage of CISC is that microprogramming is as easy as assembly language to implement, and much less expensive than hardwiring a control unit
As each CISC instruction became more capable, fewer instructions could be used to implement a given task, which made more efficient use of the relatively slow main memory
Because micro-program instruction sets can be written to match the constructs of high-level languages, the CISC compiler does not have to be as complicated
A disadvantage of CISC is that complex instructions are infrequently used by programmers and compilers
In CISC, memory references, loads and stores are slow and account for a significant fraction of all instructions
Procedure and function calls are a major CISC bottleneck: passing arguments, storing and retrieving values in registers
The CISC instruction set and chip of new generation hardware become more complex with each generation of computers
A CISC could multiply 5 by 10 with three instructions: Mov ax,10 then Mov bx,5 then Mul bx
The first RISC projects came from IBM, Stanford and UC-Berkeley in the late 70s and early 80s
The IBM 801, Stanford MIPS, and Berkeley RISC 1 and 2 were all designed with the philosophy that became known as RISC
Three main factors affect processor performance: how fast you can crank up the clock, how much work you can do per cycle, and how many instructions you need to perform a task
Instead of the one complex instruction MULT A, B, RISC breaks the operation into LOAD R1, A then LOAD R2, B then MUL R3, R1, R2 then STORE R3, C
Although more instructions are required in RISC, each executes very quickly
RISC is called reduced because of the reduction of work performed by an instruction
RISC is a type of microprocessor architecture that utilizes a small, highly-optimized set of instructions rather than a more specialized set of instructions
RISC's original goal was to limit the number of instructions on the chip so that each could be allocated enough transistors to make it execute in one cycle
The small instruction set of a typical RISC processor consists mostly of register-to-register operations, with only simple load and store operations for memory access

In RISC each operand is brought into a processor register with a load instruction, all computations are done among the data stored in processor registers, and results are transferred to memory by means of store instructions
The RISC concept is to break an operation into simpler sub-operations, such as load X, load Y, add X and Y, store Z
RISC uses only a few addressing modes because almost all its instructions have simple register addressing, though other modes such as immediate operands may be included

By using a relatively simple instruction format the RISC instruction length can be fixed and aligned on word boundaries, and an important aspect of the RISC instruction format is that it is easy to decode
RISC uses shorter instructions, breaking a complex instruction into several short simpler instructions
RISC has the ability to execute one instruction per clock cycle, done by overlapping the fetch, decode and execute phases of two or three instructions using pipelining
The advantage of register storage over memory storage is that registers can transfer information to other registers much faster than information can be transferred to and from memory
RISC has relatively few instructions, relatively few addressing modes, memory access limited to load and store instructions, and can run several instructions simultaneously
Properties of a RISC processor: simple primitive instructions and addressing modes, and instructions that execute in one clock cycle
RISC uses uniform length instructions and a fixed instruction format, and instructions interface with memory via fixed mechanisms, load and store
RISC uses pipelining and hardwired control, and complexity is pushed to the compiler
RISC processors often achieve 2 to 4 times the performance of CISC processors using comparable semiconductor technology and the same clock rates
Because the instruction set of a RISC processor is so simple it uses up much less chip space and has simple hardware requirements
RISC processors have a shorter design cycle: being simpler they can be designed more quickly, and can complete their work in 1 clock cycle

A RISC disadvantage is code quality: performance depends greatly on the code being executed, and if the programmer or compiler schedules instructions poorly the processor can spend time stalling, waiting for the result of one instruction before proceeding with a subsequent one
A RISC disadvantage is code expansion: since CISC machines perform complex actions with a single instruction where RISC may require multiple instructions for the same action
RISC machines require very fast memory systems to feed their instructions, so RISC-based systems typically contain large memory caches on the chip itself, known as a first-level cache

In the RISC instruction example the designers make sure add executes in one clock, so a compiler could multiply a and b by adding a to itself b times, using Mov ax,0 then Mov bx,10 then Mov cx,5 then a Begin label with Add ax,bx and Loop Begin
The lecture poses the in-class question: why is pipelining more difficult in CISC processors?
Pipelining is more difficult in CISC processors because instructions have varying lengths and execution times, making it harder to process instructions uniformly through the pipeline stages
Instructions utilize more cycles in CISC than in RISC, and CISC has more complex instructions than RISC
CISC typically has fewer instructions than RISC, and CISC implementations tend to be slower than RISC implementations
RISC design is approximately twice as cost-effective as CISC
RISC architectures are designed for a good cost to performance ratio, whereas CISC architectures are designed for good performance on slow memories
